paras: The Wilmington Third Ward election riot was a fight between a white crowd and a party of Black men near the Third Ward polls in Wilmington, Delaware, on the afternoon of election day, November 7, 1882. Several men in the crowd were shot, a Black man named Lewis Woodland had his skull fractured by a stone, and three Black men were later charged with riot. The local Republican paper said the whites began the fight, while the Associated Press dispatch printed across the country called the Black men the assailants.

Voting in Wilmington passed with little fighting until after 4 o'clock, when several rows broke out at the polls, including a fight at Ninth and Shipley streets in the Fifth Ward that the Daily Republican said white men started. The wire dispatch also noted trouble at the Seventh Ward polls.

According to the Wilmington Daily Republican, about 4:30 p.m. some 15 Black men, apparently from the Fifth Ward, walked down Madison Street in double file and were halted by the crowd around the Third Ward polls as they turned out Maryland Avenue. The paper said "the rough element" took this as a signal, and that "the whites" started a row in which a Black man was knocked down with a large stone. When police tried to quiet the crowd, rioters seized Officer Blackburn's club and beat him, though he captured one of his attackers.

The Black men came back with reinforcements, about 30 strong and armed with revolvers, and fired several times into the crowd at Second and Madison streets. The crowd then charged and routed them, and "a howling crowd" chased them for several squares before they got away. Charles Groves, Barney Devlin, Wilmer Barton, a man named Eagan and another named Doran were treated for cuts and gunshot wounds at Dilworth's drug store, Barton badly hurt in the side. Lewis Woodland, a Black man of East Fifth Street, was struck by a stone that shattered his frontal bone and exposed the brain, and Richard T. Davis, George Blest and Robert West suffered lesser injuries.

Several rioters were arrested, and on November 13 Mayor John P. Wales publicly thanked Officer Blackburn for his courage in making an arrest that afternoon. Woodland was reported slowly recovering a week after the riot.

On November 22 Woodland, Charles Moore and Alonzo Greenwood, all Black, were arraigned in the County Court for riot on election day. Woodland pleaded guilty without counsel, and Judge Houston fined him $20 and costs, saying the sentence would have been much heavier had he not been so badly injured. At Greenwood's trial only constable William Hickman identified him in the crowd, the defense questioned Hickman's drinking that day, and his parents testified he was home drunk; the jury acquitted him at 8 p.m. The next morning the Attorney-General abandoned the case against Moore, and no prosecution of any member of the white crowd appears in the coverage.

The Daily Republican headlined its report "A Blot in the Third Ward" and placed the start of the fight on "the whites", while describing the Black men's armed return as a surprise attack on the crowd. The Associated Press dispatch from Wilmington, carried on November 8 by the Washington National Republican, the Evening Star, the Savannah Morning News and the Knoxville Daily Chronicle, reversed this, saying the negroes "were the assailants" and the whites "retaliated" with bricks and stones. The wire named only white wounded, William Barton and Martin Fagan, and a woman shot in the breast, and did not mention Woodland.

Two days later the Springfield Weekly Republican, in a roundup of trouble at the polls, repeated that the Black men attacked the whites "with knives and pistols." Both Wilmington dailies reported the riot trial at length.

Accounts differ on who started the fight: the Daily Republican blamed the whites, the wire blamed the Black men, and the trial witness John W. Carey said about 20 Black men with clubs hustled people at the polls and began it. The wounded men named Wilmer Barton and Eagan in the local report appear as William Barton and Martin Fagan in the wire.

accounts.label: Local Republican paper
accounts.gist: About 15 peaceful Black men were blocked by the crowd at the Third Ward polls; the whites started a row and stoned one; the Black men returned about 30 strong with revolvers, fired into the crowd, and were routed and chased.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: After the polls closed the negroes, 'who were the assailants', used pistols freely and the whites answered with bricks and stones; two white men and a woman were shot.

accounts.label: State's witness at trial
accounts.gist: John W. Carey testified that a gang of about 20 Black men with clubs marched down and hustled the people around the polls, started a fight, and were overpowered by the white people and ran.

framing.detail: The Wilmington Daily Republican headlined 'A Blot in the Third Ward' and said the whites started the row, yet called the Black men's return 'with reinforcements' a surprise attack.
Papers from Washington to Savannah and Knoxville ran the AP line that the negroes 'were the assailants'; the Evening Star headed it 'RIOT IN WILMINGTON, DEL.'
The Springfield Weekly Republican's roundup said the negroes 'attacked the whites' with knives and pistols and the whites 'retaliated with brickbats'.
